Remember one distinction: dentists capture impressions and place restorations; technicians make and repair them. A successful restoration depends on both the clinical plan and the technician's craft.

A common path is: study dental technology → begin as a laboratory apprentice or assistant → master casting, waxing, ceramic layering, and grinding → learn CAD/CAM and 3D printing → advance into digital design, quality inspection, or laboratory supervision.

This field suits people with skilled hands, careful attention, aesthetic judgment, and patience for seated work. If you can make a restoration fit precisely, align the bite, and resemble a natural tooth, the work can suit you.

Dental Laboratory Technicians use dentist-provided impressions and prescriptions to make and repair dentures, crowns, bridges, and orthodontic appliances. Their work includes model casting, waxing, metal casting, ceramic layering, grinding, and polishing, with growing use of CAD/CAM and 3D printing.

entries: Dental Laboratory Technicians use dentists' impressions and prescriptions to make and repair dentures, crowns, bridges, other dental prostheses, and orthodontic appliances through processes such as model pouring, waxing, casting, porcelain application, grinding, and polishing.
Cast plaster working models from impressions.
Create wax patterns, cast metal frameworks, and fabricate crown copings.
Layer, fire, and stain ceramic to reproduce natural tooth form and shade.
Grind and polish finished work, then verify occlusion and marginal fit.
Operate CAD/CAM design and CNC fabrication equipment.
Track order progress and manage materials and quality records.

paragraphs: Begin by reviewing the day's orders and sorting all-ceramic crowns from cases that need metal frameworks. Cast models and form wax patterns in the morning, refining cusps and grooves under magnification. Layer and fire ceramic in the afternoon. After firing, grind and polish each restoration, check the bite with articulating paper, revise any poor fit, then record, inspect, and ship completed orders.
In one sentence: make, repair, and adjust teeth. Dental Laboratory Technicians cast models, shape wax, cast frameworks, layer ceramic, grind, polish, design digitally, and inspect quality.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), about 35,200 Dental Laboratory Technicians were employed in 2024, declining to a projected 33,600 by 2034. That represents about 1,600 fewer jobs, with roughly 3,900 openings per year. Median annual pay was about $48,300 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI and digital equipment will not eliminate Dental Laboratory Technicians, but they will take over scanning, design, and volume production. CAD/CAM and 3D printing handle standardization. Technicians personalize shape, occlusion, and shade through precise finishing.

paragraphs: A score of 5/10 places Dental Laboratory Technicians in the moderate AI exposure range. Digital systems take over scanning, design, and order management, while people retain fine handwork and personalized restoration.

Moderate exposure does not mean unemployment. CAD/CAM and 3D printing reduce the cost of standard crowns and bridges. Complex cases, personalized restorations, and aesthetic work increase the value of manual expertise. Technicians who combine craft with digital design have the strongest prospects.

Study dental technology and build fundamentals in model casting, waxing, and ceramic layering. Learn CAD/CAM and 3D printing at the same time. Technicians who combine hand skills with equipment fluency are most competitive.
Learn digital design software and 3D printing. Let machines handle repetitive production, then specialize in personalized restoration and advanced ceramic work. Do not stop at plaster casting.

An art or craft background helps career changers. Begin as a laboratory apprentice, learn model casting and waxing, then add digital skills. A portfolio of completed all-ceramic crowns and bridges is more useful than a list of process names.
Test manual skill during hiring through waxing and ceramic layering. Prioritize craftspeople who also use CAD/CAM, and invest in digital training to improve yield.

paragraphs: The main career risk is not overnight replacement by AI, but remaining in high-volume manual work as CAD/CAM makes standard crowns cheaper. Move toward personalized restoration and aesthetic porcelain work while adding digital skills. Use this guidance for career exploration only, not diagnosis, hiring, or employment decisions.

The greatest occupational risk is not AI but digitization and less visible competition. CAD/CAM and 3D printing are taking over high-volume denture production, favoring technicians who can design digitally while intensifying competition for technicians who rely only on hand waxing and porcelain work. Dust exposure and prolonged sitting also require attention.
